questions.knowledge_point: Identifying Parts of an Orthogonal Diagonalization
questions.problem:
$$
P=[\begin{aligned}\,∗\, & \frac{2}{3} & -\frac{2}{3} \\ \,∗\, & \frac{2}{3} & \frac{1}{3} \\ \,∗\, & \frac{1}{3} & \frac{2}{3}\end{aligned}]
$$

Consider the matrix $P$ shown above. Given that $A=PD{P}^{T}$ is an orthogonal diagonalization of a $3\times 3$ symmetric matrix $A$ for some diagonal matrix $D,$ which of the following could be the first column of the matrix $P?$
questions.worked_solution:
Recall that a matrix $A$ is orthogonally diagonalizable if there exists an orthogonal matrix $P$ such that

$$
A=PD{P}^{T},
$$

where $D$ is a diagonal matrix.

Moreover, a matrix $A$ is orthogonally diagonalizable if and only if it is symmetric.

Since  $A=PD{P}^{T}$ is an orthogonal diagonalization of a $3\times 3$ symmetric matrix $A,$ the matrix $P$ must be a $3\times 3$ orthogonal matrix. This means that 

- the first column must be orthogonal to the second and third columns, and

- the norm of the first column must be equal to $1.$

Among the given options, only the vector $[\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{3} \\ -\frac{2}{3} \\ \frac{2}{3}\end{aligned}]$ has both properties.

questions.knowledge_point: Orthogonally Diagonalizing a 3x3 Matrix With Distinct Eigenvalues
questions.problem:
$$
A=[\begin{aligned}1 & 2 & 3 \\ 2 & 2 & 2 \\ 3 & 2 & 1\end{aligned}],\,D=[\begin{aligned}0 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & -2 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 6\end{aligned}]
$$

Consider the matrices shown above. 
Given that $D={P}^{T}\,AP,$ where $P$ is an orthogonal matrix, which of the following could be the third column of the matrix $P?$
questions.worked_solution:
Recall that a matrix $A$ is orthogonally diagonalizable if there exists an orthogonal matrix $P$ such that

$$
A=PD{P}^{T},
$$

where $D$ is a diagonal matrix. Equivalently,

$$
D={P}^{T}AP.
$$

Moreover, a matrix $A$ is orthogonally diagonalizable if and only if it is symmetric.

First, note that $A$ is symmetric and $D$ is diagonal. Therefore, $D={P}^{T}\,AP$ gives an orthogonal diagonalization of $A.$

From the diagonal matrix $D$ we deduce that the eigenvalues of the matrix $A$ are ${\lambda }_{1}=0,$ ${\lambda }_{2}=-2,$ and ${\lambda }_{3}=6.$ So, the third column of $P$ corresponds to the eigenvalue ${\lambda }_{3}=6.$ 

Now, we need to find an eigenvector that corresponds to ${\lambda }_{3}=6.$ Computing $A-6I,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}A-6I & =[\begin{aligned}1 & 2 & 3 \\ 2 & 2 & 2 \\ 3 & 2 & 1\end{aligned}]-6[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}-5 & 2 & 3 \\ 2 & -4 & 2 \\ 3 & 2 & -5\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Seeking a non-zero solution of $(A-6I)x=0$ gives the eigenvector 

$$
{v}_{3}=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 1 \\ 1\end{aligned}],
$$

where $‖{v}_{3}‖=\sqrt{3}.$ Dividing ${v}_{3}$ by its norm, we obtain the third column of $P:$ 

$$
\frac{{v}_{3}}{‖{v}_{3}‖}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{3}}[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 1 \\ 1\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}\frac{\sqrt{3}}{3} \\ \frac{\sqrt{3}}{3} \\ \frac{\sqrt{3}}{3}\end{aligned}]
$$

questions.knowledge_point: Orthogonally Diagonalizing a 3x3 Matrix With Repeated Eigenvalues
questions.problem:
$$
A=[\begin{aligned}3 & 2 & 4 \\ 2 & 0 & 2 \\ 4 & 2 & 3\end{aligned}],\,D=[\begin{aligned}-1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & -1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 8\end{aligned}]
$$

Consider the matrices shown above. 
Given that $D={P}^{T}\,AP,$ where $P$ is an orthogonal matrix, which of the following could be the first and second columns of the matrix $P?$
questions.worked_solution:
Recall that a matrix $A$ is orthogonally diagonalizable if there exists an orthogonal matrix $P$ such that

$$
A=PD{P}^{T},
$$

where $D$ is a diagonal matrix. Equivalently,

$$
D={P}^{T}AP.
$$

Moreover, a matrix $A$ is orthogonally diagonalizable if and only if it is symmetric.

First, note that $A$ is symmetric and $D$ is diagonal. Therefore, $D={P}^{T}\,AP$ gives an orthogonal diagonalization of $A.$

From the diagonal matrix $D$ we deduce that the eigenvalues of the matrix $A$ are ${\lambda }_{1}=-1,$ ${\lambda }_{2}=-1,$ and ${\lambda }_{3}=8.$ So, the first and second columns of $P$ correspond to the eigenvalue ${\lambda }_{1}=-1.$ 

Now, we need to find an eigenvector that corresponds to ${\lambda }_{1}={\lambda }_{2}=-1.$ Computing $A-(-1)I,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}A-(-1)I & =[\begin{aligned}3 & 2 & 4 \\ 2 & 0 & 2 \\ 4 & 2 & 3\end{aligned}]+[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}4 & 2 & 4 \\ 2 & 1 & 2 \\ 4 & 2 & 4\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Seeking a non-zero solution of $(A-(-1)I)x=0$ gives two eigenvectors: 

$\,$ ${v}_{1}=[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 0 \\ 1\end{aligned}]\,$ and $\,{v}_{2}=[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 2 \\ 0\end{aligned}]$

Notice that eigenvectors ${v}_{1}$ and ${v}_{2}$ are not orthogonal. So, we proceed using the Gram-Schmidt process. We set 

$$
{e}_{1}={v}_{1}=[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 0 \\ 1\end{aligned}],
$$

and we find ${e}_{2}$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{e}_{2} & ={v}_{2}-\frac{{v}_{2}\cdot {e}_{1}}{{e}_{1}\cdot {e}_{1}}{e}_{1} \\  & ={v}_{2}-\frac{1}{2}{e}_{1} \\  & =[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 2 \\ 0\end{aligned}]-\frac{1}{2}[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 0 \\ 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}-\frac{1}{2} \\ 2 \\ -\frac{1}{2}\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, dividing ${e}_{1}$ and ${e}_{2}$ by their respective norms, we obtain the first and second columns of $P:$ 

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{{e}_{1}}{‖{e}_{1}‖} & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 0 \\ 1\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}-\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2} \\ 0 \\ \frac{\sqrt{2}}{2}\end{aligned}] \\ \frac{{e}_{2}}{‖{e}_{2}‖} & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{\frac{9}{2}}}[\begin{aligned}-\frac{1}{2} \\ 2 \\ -\frac{1}{2}\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}-\frac{\sqrt{2}}{6} \\ \frac{2\sqrt{2}}{3} \\ -\frac{\sqrt{2}}{6}\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

questions.knowledge_point: Orthogonally Diagonalizing a 3x3 Matrix With Repeated Eigenvalues
questions.problem:
$$
A=[\begin{aligned}7 & -1 & 2 \\ -1 & 7 & -2 \\ 2 & -2 & 10\end{aligned}],\,D=[\begin{aligned}6 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 6 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 12\end{aligned}]
$$

Consider the matrices shown above. 
Given that $D={P}^{T}\,AP,$ where $P$ is an orthogonal matrix, which of the following could be the first and second columns of the matrix $P?$
questions.worked_solution:
Recall that a matrix $A$ is orthogonally diagonalizable if there exists an orthogonal matrix $P$ such that

$$
A=PD{P}^{T},
$$

where $D$ is a diagonal matrix. Equivalently,

$$
D={P}^{T}AP.
$$

Moreover, a matrix $A$ is orthogonally diagonalizable if and only if it is symmetric.

First, note that $A$ is symmetric and $D$ is diagonal. Therefore, $D={P}^{T}\,AP$ gives an orthogonal diagonalization of $A.$

From the diagonal matrix $D$ we deduce that the eigenvalues of the matrix $A$ are ${\lambda }_{1}=6,$ ${\lambda }_{2}=6,$ and ${\lambda }_{3}=12.$ So, the first and second columns of $P$ correspond to the eigenvalues ${\lambda }_{1}$ and ${\lambda }_{2}.$ 

Now, we need to find eigenvectors that correspond to ${\lambda }_{1}={\lambda }_{2}=6.$ Computing $A-6I,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}A-6I & =[\begin{aligned}7 & -1 & 2 \\ -1 & 7 & -2 \\ 2 & -2 & 10\end{aligned}]-6[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}1 & -1 & 2 \\ -1 & 1 & -2 \\ 2 & -2 & 4\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Seeking a non-zero solution of $(A-6I)x=0$ gives two eigenvectors: 

$\,$ ${v}_{1}=[\begin{aligned}-2 \\ 0 \\ 1\end{aligned}]\,$ and $\,{v}_{2}=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 1 \\ 0\end{aligned}]$

Notice that eigenvectors ${v}_{1}$ and ${v}_{2}$ are not orthogonal. So, we proceed using the Gram-Schmidt process. We set 

$$
{e}_{1}={v}_{1}=[\begin{aligned}-2 \\ 0 \\ 1\end{aligned}],
$$

and we find ${e}_{2}$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{e}_{2} & ={v}_{2}-\frac{{v}_{2}\cdot {e}_{1}}{{e}_{1}\cdot {e}_{1}}{e}_{1} \\  & ={v}_{2}+\frac{2}{5}{e}_{1} \\  & =[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 1 \\ 0\end{aligned}]+\frac{2}{5}[\begin{aligned}-2 \\ 0 \\ 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{5} \\ 1 \\ \frac{2}{5}\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, dividing ${e}_{1}$ and ${e}_{2}$ by their respective norms, we obtain the first and second columns of $P:$ 

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{{e}_{1}}{‖{e}_{1}‖} & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{5}}[\begin{aligned}-2 \\ 0 \\ 1\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}-\frac{2\sqrt{5}}{5} \\ 0 \\ \frac{\sqrt{5}}{5}\end{aligned}] \\ \frac{{e}_{2}}{‖{e}_{2}‖} & =\frac{1}{(\frac{\sqrt{30}}{5})}[\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{5} \\ 1 \\ \frac{2}{5}\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}\frac{\sqrt{30}}{30} \\ \frac{\sqrt{30}}{6} \\ \frac{\sqrt{30}}{15}\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$
